source.title: Why is SAM Robust to Label Noise?
source.authors: Christina Baek; Zico Kolter; Aditi Raghunathan

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study compares training methods and explicit regularization on held-out performance under label noise, a different setting and method from the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study measures test accuracy and training behavior on label-noisy data. It does not test the listed versions’ natural-label, architecture, adaptive-optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-measure, or memorized-example claims. Figure-only comparisons are not transcribed as numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study tests mechanisms of SAM's robustness to partial label corruption, rather than any listed version. Its width sweep does not establish interpolation or training to convergence, and its Hessian-trace comparison does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or the generalization gap.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the neural-network results: Jacobian perturbation preserves nearly all of SAM's label-noise advantage, while explicit final-layer weight and activation regularization recovers only part. The broader conclusion also distinguishes linear models, where preferential up-weighting of low-loss examples explains the benefit, and emphasizes learning clean examples before fitting noise rather than flatness at convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Studies 1-SAM and variants, along with an explicit regularization inspired by its Jacobian effect, under synthetic label corruption; the listed claim versions concern other comparisons and settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Label-noise presence changes the reported relative gains: the proposed regularization improves test accuracy by 8% with label noise, while under no label noise it improves by 1% after hyperparameter search. The authors also report that results vary with perturbation magnitude and training time.

fits_no_version.finding: With 30% CIFAR10 label corruption, best test accuracy is 69.47% for 1-SAM, 69.17% for J-SAM, 54.13% for L-SAM, 52.48% for SGD, and 60.8% for regularized SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jacobian perturbation preserves nearly all of 1-SAM's label-noise robustness; logit-only perturbation does not, and explicit weight and activation regularization recovers part of the advantage.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 13 reports that both SAM and SGD improve as ResNet18 width increases under 30% label corruption, without identifying the interpolation threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing ResNet18 width improves performance in this noisy-label training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix B.2 reports no correlation between test accuracy and Hessian trace in toy linear models; n-SAM can finish with a smaller trace and lower test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian trace does not reliably track test accuracy across these SAM variants in noisy linear classification.

record.problems: The reported table gives no uncertainty estimates. Several comparisons are shown only in figures, with no textual numerical values. The main CIFAR10 setup replaces Batch Norm with Layer Norm for 1-SAM; results are from a label-corruption setting and do not establish the listed natural-label claims.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only comparisons in Figures 1–4 and 7–14, including toy Gaussian data, other datasets, no-label-noise results, data-size and model-width sweeps, are not assigned numerical values because the text gives no corresponding values. The text describes some of these trends, but they are outside the listed claim versions and the table rows capture the directly quantified CIFAR10 comparison.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fully random-label training, near-perfect random-label fitting, and chance-level held-out accuracy under random labels.

Whether widening beyond the width needed for zero training error continues lowering test error. Figure 13 reports improvement with width but does not locate that threshold or establish convergence; training also uses weight decay.
Controlled comparisons of convolutional and fully connected networks, including the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Dropout's effect on held-out error and its dependence on data size, dropout strength, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus generalization gaps among convolutional networks with similarly low training loss, including ranking against norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing examples selected by memorization influence versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tests/T2 classification conflicts with its correctly unlinked rows. Figure-only findings can be assessed from explicit textual descriptions, but the width and Hessian-trace findings still do not measure V2 or V7. They were declared in rows_left_out, so they do not require missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit versus natural-label generalization and chance-level test accuracy.
Test error across widths beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of tuning, weight decay, or switching optimizers.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout’s effect on held-out error and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Whether magnitude-aware sharpness tracks the train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: 1-SAM (ρ = 0.01)
rows.operation_detail: Train with 1-SAM on CIFAR10 with 30% label corruption; report best test accuracy.
rows.note: Label-noise setting; does not measure a listed claim version.
rows.check: The numerical comparison is correct, but measures SAM's label-noise robustness rather than a listed version.

rows.subject: L-SAM (ρ = 0.01)
rows.operation_detail: Train with SAM perturbation applied to the logit scale term on CIFAR10 with 30% label corruption; report best test accuracy.
rows.note: Authors describe marginal early-stopping gains over SGD; label-noise setting.
rows.check: The numerical comparison is correct. The small improvement over SGD cannot be classified as partial evidence for any listed version.

rows.subject: J-SAM (ρ = 0.01)
rows.operation_detail: Train with SAM perturbation applied to the Jacobian term on CIFAR10 with 30% label corruption; report best test accuracy.
rows.note: Authors say J-SAM recovers almost all of 1-SAM’s gains; label-noise setting.
rows.check: The numerical comparison is correct. Recovering SAM's gains through Jacobian perturbation does not establish any listed version.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.operation_detail: Train on CIFAR10 with 30% label corruption; report best test accuracy.
rows.note: Reference method for the table’s comparisons.
rows.check: Correct baseline value, but this standalone comparator does not test a listed version.

rows.subject: SGD w/ Proposed Reg
rows.operation_detail: Train with ℓ2 regularization on last-layer weights and last hidden-layer activations on CIFAR10 with 30% label corruption; report best test accuracy.
rows.note: Authors state the proposed regularization closes the gap from 17% to 9%; label-noise setting.
rows.check: Correct value for the study's proposed regularization method. Its improvement over SGD is outside the listed versions, so partial is not an applicable claim state.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
